newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia wool prices seen rising to 630 c/kg - WI.
newsitem.headline: Australia wool prices seen rising to 630 c/kg - WI.

text.p: Wool International (WI), the statutory body in charge of selling Australia's 1.8 million bale wool stockpile, forecast the average Australian wool price in 1997/98 will exceed average prices in the current season to June 30.
WI forecast in its latest Insight newsletter that the average eastern market indicator (EMI) price in 1997/98 would be 630 cents a kg in a range of plus/minus 100 cents.
Its forecast EMI for 1996/97 is unchanged at 600 cents a kg. This is on the assumption that prices remain at around current levels in the final quarter of the current season, it said.
The EMI rose by three cents to 626 cents a kg clean at the latest auction, held last Thursday.
A key consideration in the forecast of 630 cents for 1997/98 was that demand from China would remain steady at its current high level, WI said.
It was also based on a belief that economic conditions would improve in Western Europe, leading to stronger consumption growth.
Additionally, it was expected that woolgrower and WI stocks would flow onto the market in response to increasing prices, limiting the extent of the price rise, WI said.
While China's textile industry slowed in 1996 on weaker export demand, the outlook there was optimistic, WI said.

An anticipated relaxation of monetary policy was likely to encourage spending and activity, it said. Gross domestic product growth is forecast at more than 10 percent in the next two years, with inflation remaining under control.
"A factor contributing to stronger growth is anticipated growth in world demand, especially in key export markets," WI said.
Consumer expenditure continues to grow at a markedly faster rate than in traditional wool consuming countries, it said.

Currently Chinese wool consumption per head was very low but the rapidly expanding consumer base of middle income earners offered significant potential as a high growth market for wool apparel consumption, it said.
On supply issues, WI said estimated Australian grower stock increased by 76 million kg, or almost 417,000 bales, in 1995/96.
Some stock rundown occurred in 1996/97, increasing supply to the market.
With February-June the traditional stock rundown period, the average rundown rate between 1991/92 and 1994/95 was 54 percent.
This season good grain prices had enabled mixed enterprises to withhold wool from sale until prices improved. The rundown rate this year was assumed to be in the 44-54 percent range, WI said.
The total rundown for 1996/97 could be in the range of 40-50 million kg, it said.
In 1997/98, assuming prices gradually improve over the season, WI anticipates about 30 million kg of grower stock could be released.
